newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British Energy achieves 1st yr profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British Energy achieves 1st yr profit.

text.p: Britain's nuclear power generator British Energy Plc on Wednesday reported a profit in its first annual results since its controversial privatisation last year.

It also announced a 1.5 billion pound ($2.4 billion) service contract with state-owned British Nuclear Fuels (BNFL) that it said would cap the company's liabilities and cut fuel costs, leading to a saving of around 10 million pounds this year.
"We're only nine months old. We're out of nappies now," chief executive Robert Hawley said in an interview.

The company achieved profits of 61 million pounds in the year to March 31, 1997, compared with a pro forma loss of 155 million the previous year. It also reported a total dividend of 13.7 pence a share, as forecast in its flotation prospectus.
"The message of this year's results is that we've delivered what we said we would in the prospectus," Hawley added.
The figures sparked strong buying of British Energy shares which stood at 148 pence, up nine pence on the day. By 1200 GMT, more than 10 million shares had changed hands.
"The figures were in line with the expectations but there are a lot of people out there who think the stock is undervalued," one trader said.

British Energy, which provides around 20 percent of the UK's electricity supply, is the holding company for Nuclear Electric (NE) and Scottish Nuclear (SN), the two nuclear electricity generating companies.
The deal announced on Wednesday means BNFL will provide the fuel for NE's five advanced gas-cooled reactor (AGR) stations as well as handle the spent fuel.

A BNFL spokesman the deal was "basically an extension" of an existing contract with NE, extending the period to cover the entire lives of the stations to 2006. There is also a facility to extend it further if the lives of the stations warranted it.
The reprocessing agreement is similar to one concluded two years ago between BNFL and SN.

For British Energy, the new contracts together with those in place already, means the company now has fixed price contracts -- subject only to RPI indexation -- covering the bulk of spent fuel services for the lives of its seven AGR power stations. Apart from the AGRs, it also operates the Sizewell pressurised water reactor.
"(The BNFL deal) caps the majority of our remaining liabilities," said Hawley. "It means that we can reduce our fuel costs straight away some 10 million pounds in the current year".

A shaky start to British Energy's flotation last year -- just days after the temporary closure of two of its eight modern power stations -- saw its shares debut below the 105 pence at which they were sold to institutions on a partly-paid basis.
The second tranche of 98 pence is to be paid in September.
The share has subsequently recovered, mainly on the back of a 10 percent jump in output last year.

Hawley warned, however, that output was unlikely to be as strong in the current year because seven statutory outages -- which have to be carried out every two or three years -- are set for this year, as against four last year.
"We'll be struggling to meet the same output this year," he added.
In the year to March, the company produced 67.21 Terawatt hours. A Terawatt is the largest unit of measurement for electricity sales, representing one billion kilowatt hours.

British Energy took its first venture outside the nuclear power generation field in April when it purchased a 12.5 percent stake in Humber Power Ltd's gas-fired power plant. Hawley said the company would continue to look for principally joint venture deals both in Britain and internationally.

Last October the company announced a restructuring programme to cut jobs over the next three years to achieve savings of 50 million pounds a year. Hawley said the workforce was reduced by 484 to 5,940 last year and it was anticipated it would be cut further to below 5,000 by March, 2000. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
